newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's new leader begins forming cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's new leader begins forming cabinet.

text.p: Ecuador's new President Fabian Alarcon began forming his cabinet on Thursday and urged his countrymen to be patient on the road to economic recovery.

He named economist Carlos Davalos as finance minister. A veteran politician, Davalos is deputy director of the small centre-right Alfarist Radical Front led by Alarcon but little is known about his economic credentials.
The president, elected by Congress on Tuesday to serve until August 1998, also named Gen. Ramiro Ricaute as defence minister and Eduardo Alcivar as health minister.
"Our cabinet is the product of dialogue and consensus," he said in a brief public ceremony.

Alarcon, 49, replaced populist Abdala Bucaram who was ousted by the legislature a week ago for "mental incompetence," sparking a political crisis that saw three people claiming the presidency on constitutional grounds.
Elaborating on his first message to Ecuadoreans after he was sworn in, Alarcon asked for "understanding, patience," saying his government would not rush into taking "hasty measures."
Under Bucaram's rule "gas rates changed every day," he said, stressing that he would govern with "seriousness" under "a national dialogue that means convince not impose."
But some analysts speculated Alarcon would be hard-pressed to convince impoverished Ecuadoreans that more economic hardship is good for them.

"He assumed power riding a wave of protests against austerity measures so he is going to find it extremely difficult to say, well, these measures are needed," Santiago Nieto, director of consulting firm Informe Confidencial, said.
Militant labour unions, which drew hundreds of thousands of protesters into the streets last week, indicated they would give the new administration little room for manoeuvre.

"We'll remain vigilant to see if the people's demands are met. If that is not the case we'll resume our protests," Fausto Duran, head of the United Workers' Front, Ecuador's largest labour union, told Reuters.
Amid reports of large-scale corruption during Bucaram's six-month rule, the new administration began to look closely into financial accounts and a bloated public sector.
"We are detecting about 10,000 people that were contracted in the public sector by the sole virtue of political patronage," Interior Minister Cesar Verduga said.
Meanwhile, Bucaram continued a regional tour to win support. He arrived in Argentina on Thursday and again denounced the "coup d'etat" that he said toppled him.
"I am going to legally expose matters and the whole world will understand that there is cowardice in being silent about a coup d'etat," he told reporters at Buenos Aires airport.
He was scheduled to meet Argentine President Carlos Menem, his strongest supporter in the region, who said on Wednesday that Alarcon was leading a "de facto" government.
Bucaram, who was accompanied by one of his sons, said: "Nobody beat me in an election. Four people cannot ruin a constitution in a minute."
